CC @berarma

This issue was previously discussed in #102982, but it appears to be unrelated to the crash that was resolved with #103077. This issue includes some additional debugging info beyond the conversation in the previous issue. Also, I converted the MRP to a 30fps video, which still shows the issue. I find this to be convincing that it is not solely a performance issue.

Based on previous discussions, this issue is likely only reproducible on Windows and not MacOS or Linux.
I think I found the cause of this issue. `video_ready = true;` should be set regardless of whether `(next_frame_time > comp_time)` is true. I'll submit a PR shortly.

> I think I found the cause of this issue. `video_ready = true;` should be set regardless of whether `(next_frame_time > comp_time)` is true. I'll submit a PR shortly.

That would disable frame skipping, but this isn't always desired.

Does it improve if vsync is disabled?

Please, could you build rc1 with [this patch](https://github.com/user-attachments/files/18904519/0001-Print-video-timings.patch.txt) and post the console output for the 144fps and 30fps videos?

I observed in the videos you uploaded that the video played on beta3 plays slower than the video played on rc1. I think rc1 is skipping frames to keep up with the framerate instead of playing the video at a lower speed. This is correct behavior in rc1, but I don't understand why you get the same with the 30fps video so there must be something else.

As I was debugging this, I noticed another issue -- on looping videos, the first or last frame is rendered as transparent. I bisected this to commit 032cec5 as well. I'll submit it as a separate issue with more info later, but it is possible it shares a common cause with this issue.

> That would disable frame skipping, but this isn't always desired.

I think in that case, frame skipping must be broken, see my results with vsync below.

> Does it improve if vsync is disabled?

No, despite my framerate in the logs going up to >5000.

> I observed in the videos you uploaded that the video played on beta3 plays slower than the video played on rc1.

Actually, it's the opposite. The recordings may be slightly off because I wasn't able to record from the exact start of the video. I added a timer, and with the 30fps video, beta3 plays the video in 2.843 seconds and rc1 plays the video in 2.989 seconds. With the 144fps video, beta3 plays the video in 2.938s while rc1 plays it in 3.017s. ffmpeg says the duration of both videos is exactly 3.000s.

> Please, could you build rc1 with [this patch](https://github.com/user-attachments/files/18904519/0001-Print-video-timings.patch.txt) and post the console output for the 144fps and 30fps videos?

I'm debugging the generated assembly code and I've found something very unsettling. I hope someone with better knowledge of compiler internals can look into this. It seems only optimized Windows builds are affected.

It happens inside this function:

https://github.com/godotengine/godot/blob/394508d26dcf1b7a9362453f9009c07d969f1a7e/modules/theora/video_stream_theora.cpp#L330

There's a variable `comp_time` that I'm setting at the start of the function and it doesn't change its value. The compiler seems to optimize by putting this variable into a register, and expects that register to hold that value for the rest of the function. But this function calls a C function:

https://github.com/godotengine/godot/blob/394508d26dcf1b7a9362453f9009c07d969f1a7e/thirdparty/libtheora/decode.c#L2740

This function changes some registers without preserving their values, and it might happen that it changes the register that holds the variable `comp_time` above.

I've posted here some patches that print timing information, and for that, two variables `start_time` and `end_time` are used. Something similar happens to these variables. Variable `start_time` is created at the start of the function and assigned to a register for the rest of the function, and it doesn't hold its value until the end because its register is overwritten in the same way.

Variable `end_time` is created at the end of the function and is used immediately but it's also affected. Why? Because the value `1000000.0` from the macro `USEC_TO_SEC` is also stored in a register when `start_time` is assigned a value. When  the end of the function is reached, that register no longer holds the same value and the calculation for `end_time` goes wrong.

Depending on the build, some variables might not be affected because the register they use might be different and not changed. For example, adding some printfs to the code can change the outcome, but almost always there's some variable affected.

I think the compiler is operating on the assumption that those registers won't change for the invocation of the function because it's under its control. They change in another function but it should also be under its control because it's building both. I don't really know how this should be handled.

Yup, it fixes my issues as well. I think the long term fix for this is to disable Theora assembly optimizations for `x86_64` Windows. Multiple of their functions clobber xmm6/xmm7, both using OC_X86_ASM or OC_X86_64_ASM flags.

```
--- a/platform/windows/detect.py
+++ b/platform/windows/detect.py
@@ -732,7 +732,7 @@ def configure_mingw(env: "SConsEnvironment"):
         if env["use_static_cpp"]:
             env.Append(LINKFLAGS=["-static"])

-    if env["arch"] in ["x86_32", "x86_64"]:
+    if env["arch"] == "x86_32":
         env["x86_libtheora_opt_gcc"] = True

     env.Append(CCFLAGS=["-ffp-contract=off"])
```

I've submitted this as PR #103176. Please test if you can and see if it fixes the issues for you as well. It appears to fix LTO for me, but I have not yet tested it extensively, and it may be system-dependent.

Amazingly, for me, this patch also fixes the issue of the blank frame when looping I brought up earlier in the thread.
